purpose: Research recommendations for how ORYN's counselor/product logic should interpret destination-country university admissions systems -- the layer above individual universities/programmes -- for students applying internationally. Conceptual research output only; does not modify production schema or logic.
scope_note: 6 countries covered by design (not exhaustive): United States, United Kingdom, Netherlands, Italy, Germany, Canada. Builds directly on R2.1 (secondary-education-system research, data/research/academic-systems/secondary-systems-v1.json) -- every country's qualification_eligibility section maps back to MEB/IB/AP/Cambridge/French Bac/German Abitur as researched there.
methodology_note: Each country researched independently against primary/official sources (national admissions platforms, ministries, credential-recognition bodies) wherever fetchable; secondary/consulting sources used for discovery or corroboration only, never as sole evidence for a factual claim. Every claim carries a scope label (national/platform/university/programme) and a source array. Where automated fetch was blocked (recurring across ucas.com, ouac.on.ca, anabin.kmk.org, education.gouv.fr and others), findings are flagged as secondary-corroborated rather than presented as verbatim-confirmed -- see each country's own unresolved_questions.

A_admissions_architecture.primary_application_route: There is no single national application route. The largest single platform is the Common Application (Common App), used by 1,000+ member colleges and universities including virtually all highly selective private institutions. A second, smaller platform is the Coalition for College application (approx. 150 member schools, mostly overlapping with Common App membership), which since 2023 is delivered through the Scoir platform rather than a standalone Coalition portal. In parallel, many public university systems run their own dedicated application platforms entirely outside Common App/Coalition: the University of California uses the UC Application (its own essays called 'Personal Insight Questions', its own activities list format), Texas public universities largely use ApplyTexas, the California State University system uses Cal State Apply, and SUNY schools use applySUNY. Some individual institutions — most notably MIT, which uses its own 'MyMIT' portal — accept none of the shared platforms and require applicants to apply directly through an institution-built system. A typical applicant therefore ends up using two or three different systems in parallel (e.g., Common App for private colleges + UC Application for California public schools + ApplyTexas for Texas public schools), not one.
A_admissions_architecture.centralized_or_decentralized: Decentralized. The US has no single national admissions platform, no national ministry-run allocation system, and no government body that processes or ranks applications. Common App is the dominant private, non-profit intermediary but is one option among several competing/parallel systems, and universities remain free to require their own supplemental materials or opt out of shared platforms entirely (e.g., MIT).

University of California Application (UC-specific, not shared) — admission.universityofcalifornia.edu

applySUNY (SUNY system) — suny.edu

A_admissions_architecture.direct_university_application_possible: Yes, and in a small number of cases (e.g., MIT) it is the ONLY option — the university accepts no shared platform at all. Most universities that participate in Common App or Coalition also layer significant institution-specific supplemental essays and forms on top of the shared platform, so 'direct application' and 'platform application' are not fully separable in practice — the shared platform carries the common data (biographical info, one main personal essay, activities list) while each university still collects its own supplement.
A_admissions_architecture.application_limit_if_any: Common App itself caps a single applicant account at 20 colleges per cycle (a Common App platform policy, not a US-wide legal limit). There is no higher authority capping total applications across all platforms combined — a student can apply to more than 20 institutions total by also using Coalition/Scoir, a state system, and/or direct institutional portals. Note: this 20-school Common App cap was found consistently in secondary sources (CollegeVine FAQ, AdmissionSight) that cite the Common App's own applicant-support policy; this research pass could not independently render the primary commonapp.org policy page to quote it verbatim, so treat the exact number as high-confidence but not independently source-verified in this pass.
A_admissions_architecture.parallel_application_rules: Within Common App: one core profile (biographical data, one primary personal essay, one Activities List of up to 10 entries) is reused across every college the student adds; each college can additionally require its own supplemental essays/questions layered on top of the shared core. This 'one core + per-school supplements' mechanic is the defining structural feature of the platform model. The same general pattern (shared core + institution-specific supplement) applies to Coalition/Scoir and to the state systems, but these are separate accounts/logins from Common App — a student applying to both a Common App school and a UC school maintains two entirely separate applications with no data sharing between them.

B_qualification_eligibility.recognition_mechanism: No national credential-recognition body exists for undergraduate admissions in the US (this is structurally different from, e.g., UK NARIC-style equivalency bodies used for some purposes). US undergraduate admission is legally and administratively decentralized: each university's own admissions office (often with a dedicated 'international admissions' reader or committee) independently evaluates foreign secondary credentials as part of holistic review. Some public universities and community colleges require or recommend a third-party course-by-course credential evaluation from a NACES- or AICE-accredited agency (e.g., WES, ECE) to translate foreign transcripts into a US-equivalent GPA/diploma-equivalency statement, but this is a university-level (sometimes state-system-level) practice, not a national requirement. Many selective private universities do not require external evaluation at all and instead read the original foreign transcript and school profile directly.
B_qualification_eligibility.baseline_qualification_expectation: Generally: completion of secondary education broadly equivalent to a US high school diploma (approximately 12 years of primary+secondary schooling). Universities describe this loosely (e.g., 'secondary school credential recognized in your home country as equivalent to a US high school diploma') rather than via a codified national equivalency table.
B_qualification_eligibility.subject_prerequisites_general: No national subject-prerequisite law. Individual universities/programs set their own expected or required high-school subject preparation (see subject_prerequisites section below) — this is university/programme-level, not a national admissions rule.
B_qualification_eligibility.equivalency_process: Case-by-case, institution-specific. Where used, third-party evaluators (WES, ECE, and other NACES/AICE-accredited services) are commercial organizations, not government bodies; there is no government oversight body auditing them, per multiple sourced discussions of the credential-evaluation industry. Which evaluator (if any) is accepted, and whether an evaluation is even required, is set independently by each university.
B_qualification_eligibility.university_discretion: Very high. Because there is no national credential authority, no centralized allocation algorithm, and (per NACAC's own data) admissions offices weigh a combination of grades, rigor, tests, essays, recommendations, and activities in a holistic, non-formulaic review, individual admissions offices retain broad, largely unconstrained discretion over how any given foreign credential (MEB, IB, A-Level, Bac, Abitur) is read, weighted, and compared to domestic applicants. This is a structural feature of US admissions, not an oversight gap — it follows directly from the private/decentralized nature of most selective US higher education and from the legal doctrine (well established in US case law) that private and public universities have wide latitude in setting their own admission standards.

credentials_covered.turkiye_meb: No dedicated national pathway or codified equivalency found; treated like any other foreign secondary credential under general institution-level holistic review (see turkiye_applicant_view section — most claims here are reasoned inference, not Turkey-specific sourced fact, and are labeled accordingly).
credentials_covered.ib_diploma: Well-recognized nationally in practice (widely accepted, and the IB's formal predicted-grade documentation is a known, legible artifact to US admissions readers), but 'recognition' still means each university reads and weighs it independently — there is no codified national IB-to-GPA conversion table.
credentials_covered.a_levels: Same pattern as IB: broadly familiar to US admissions offices (Cambridge/Edexcel A-Levels are a known quantity, especially for applicants from British/Commonwealth-curriculum schools), evaluated case by case, no codified national table.
credentials_covered.ap_plus_us_diploma: Native case — AP is a US domestic credential layered onto a standard US high school diploma; this is the baseline case the rest of the admissions system is implicitly built around.
credentials_covered.french_bac: Broadly recognized as a legible foreign credential by admissions offices experienced with French applicants; no codified national equivalency found in this research pass.
credentials_covered.german_abitur: Same pattern as French Bac — broadly legible to experienced international-admissions readers; no codified national equivalency found in this research pass.

turkiye_applicant_view.standard_diploma_sufficient_for_direct_e: Unknown / not confirmed from an authoritative current source in this research pass. Reasoned inference (not sourced fact): because US admissions has no national credential-recognition body and evaluates every foreign secondary credential case-by-case (see B above), a standard MEB (Turkish national curriculum) diploma is very likely, in principle, sufficient to satisfy the baseline 'secondary credential equivalent to a US high school diploma' expectation at most US universities — the open question is competitiveness, not eligibility (see eligibility_competitiveness_fit). This inference should be verified against specific target universities' international-admissions pages before being presented to a student as settled fact.
turkiye_applicant_view.additional_qualifications_commonly_requi: Not found as a national requirement. Reasoned inference: AP/IB/A-Level coursework, SAT/ACT scores (where required by the target university's current testing policy), and English-proficiency test scores (TOEFL/IELTS/Duolingo, unless exempted) are commonly ADVANTAGEOUS rather than universally REQUIRED for MEB-only applicants, consistent with the general holistic-review, course-rigor-signals-strength pattern documented for domestic applicants (NACAC data) and the general international-admissions pattern. This is inference extended from general system architecture, not a Turkey-specific sourced claim.
turkiye_applicant_view.ap_ib_a_level_impact: Reasoned inference, not directly sourced for Turkey: many Turkish private/international schools offer AP, IB, or A-Level tracks specifically because these provide (a) subject-level academic evidence that is more immediately legible to US admissions readers than raw MEB numeric grades, and (b) in the AP/IB case, a course-rigor signal that maps directly onto the 'most rigorous coursework available' criterion multiple US universities (MIT, Georgia Tech, per this research) explicitly say they look for. This plausibly increases both eligibility clarity and competitiveness for students who hold them alongside or instead of a pure MEB record, but no Turkey-specific authoritative source was found confirming this empirically.
turkiye_applicant_view.national_entrance_exam_relevance: Reasoned inference: LGS (secondary-school placement exam) and YKS (Turkish national university entrance exam) results are Turkish-system-internal instruments used to allocate placement within Turkey's own domestic higher-education system; they are not part of the US SAT/ACT/AP/IB apparatus and no evidence was found that any US university requests or uses LGS/YKS scores in undergraduate admissions decisions. This is a structural inference from how the two systems are built, not a directly sourced negative confirmation.
turkiye_applicant_view.foundation_year_common: Likely uncommon for the US pathway, in contrast to the UK (where foundation years for Turkish MEB-only applicants are a documented, named pathway at some universities, per general knowledge of UK admissions). US undergraduate admission does not have a widespread, named 'foundation year' institution comparable to UK foundation programmes; the closer US-side mechanisms are bridge/pathway programs run by some universities for underprepared international students, or English-intensive pre-sessional programs tied to language proficiency rather than academic-credential gaps. This is a reasoned structural inference, not directly sourced for Turkish applicants specifically.
turkiye_applicant_view.recognition_centralized_or_university_sp: University-specific, following directly from the fact that no national credential-recognition body exists for US undergraduate admissions generally (see B above). No evidence of any Turkey-specific national/bilateral recognition arrangement with the US was found.

sources.note: No authoritative, current, Turkey-to-US-specific admissions source was located in this research pass. Searches returned Turkey-domestic admissions information (MEB pages describing foreign credentials entering Turkey — the reverse direction) and UK-specific Turkish-applicant guidance (University of Manchester), but no equivalent official US-side or NACAC-level source addressing Turkish MEB applicants specifically. This is a genuine research gap, not an omission — see unresolved_questions.

academic_evidence_used.transcript_role: Central and mandatory. Virtually every US university requires an official secondary-school transcript covering the full multi-year academic record (not just final-year results), submitted either via the Common App 'School Report' form (completed by the counselor) or the applicable platform's equivalent, plus a 'school profile' document from the counselor's office describing the school's grading scale, curriculum, and grading distribution so the admissions reader can contextualize the numbers.
academic_evidence_used.native_grades_handling: Handled at the university's discretion. Practice varies: some universities (particularly some public universities and community colleges) recalculate a US-equivalent 4.0-scale GPA in-house or via a required third-party course-by-course credential evaluation (illustrative example: Miami University's stated 'Recalculated GPA' policy for first-year international applicants). Many selective private universities instead read the original transcript in its native grading scale alongside the school profile, without converting to a 4.0 figure, relying on trained international-admissions readers for context. This is a university-level practice, not a national standard, and ORYN should never assume a specific conversion methodology without a named, current source from the specific target university.
academic_evidence_used.predicted_grades_role: Largely not a formal, decision-driving mechanism the way UK predicted grades are (see predicted_grades section below for detail). Where predicted grades appear at all in a US application, it is generally because the applicant's own qualification (e.g., IB Diploma) issues formal predicted grades as part of its own internal process, and the student/school may include or reference them as supporting context — not because the US college's own application architecture has a formal predicted-grade input field driving a conditional offer.
academic_evidence_used.final_grades_role: Used in two structurally distinct ways: (1) as part of the holistic academic record already submitted at time of application (prior years' final grades), and (2) as an ongoing-performance check via the Common App 'Mid-Year Report' (first-semester senior grades, sent after admission decisions in many cases, though some colleges review it before decisions) and 'Final Report' (final transcript after graduation) — the final report is what admission offices use to confirm the student's admission remains valid (see conditional_vs_unconditional_admission).
academic_evidence_used.external_exams_role: AP exam scores, IB exam/Diploma results, and SAT/ACT scores where required, function as supporting/contextual academic evidence within holistic review rather than as the sole determinant. Per College Board's own AP Students site, colleges primarily value the AP COURSE (as a rigor signal reflected in the school-reported course grade) at the admissions-decision stage, while the numeric AP EXAM SCORE more commonly matters for the separate, post-enrollment credit/placement process (see standardized_tests section for the fuller distinction).
academic_evidence_used.course_rigor_signal: A named, explicit criterion at many selective universities. Illustrative language pattern: admissions offices (Georgia Tech, MIT, per this research) explicitly say they look for students who took 'the most rigorous coursework available' at their own school — AP, IB, A-Level, dual-enrollment, or honors tracks in core subjects. Common App's own School Report form asks counselors to rate the applicant's curriculum rigor relative to what the school offers. This is a widespread pattern across selective admissions, but the specific weighting is university-level, not codified nationally.
academic_evidence_used.subject_prerequisites: University/programme level — see dedicated subject_prerequisites section.
academic_evidence_used.standardized_tests: See dedicated standardized_tests section — status varies sharply by university and is currently in active flux (2026-27 cycle).

predicted_grades.are_used: Not used as a formal, structural, decision-driving input the way UK predicted grades are. US applications are generally evaluated against the actual academic record already completed at time of application (through junior year / first half of senior year), not a forward-looking predicted score for exams not yet sat.
predicted_grades.where: Where predicted grades surface at all, it is typically because the applicant's own qualification produces them as a byproduct (e.g., IB Diploma candidates receive formal, school-issued predicted grades as part of the IB's own process) and a school or student may reference them in supporting materials — not because a US college's application form has a dedicated 'predicted grade' field that determines the decision.
predicted_grades.by_whom: When present, predicted grades originate from the student's own school/qualification body (e.g., IB predicted grades issued by the school under IB rules), not from the US university.
predicted_grades.for_what: Contextual/supporting information at most, not a formal admissions-decision trigger and not a conditional-offer trigger, based on available evidence.
predicted_grades.conditional_offer_relationship: Fundamentally different mechanism from the UK. UK conditional offers are explicitly built around predicted grades (offer conditional on achieving a stated grade in a future exam). No evidence was found of an equivalent formal mechanism in mainstream US undergraduate admissions; the closer US analogue — admission being contingent on senior-year performance — is evaluated against ACTUAL final grades via the Mid-Year and Final Report, not against a pre-stated predicted-grade target (see conditional_vs_unconditional_admission).
predicted_grades.final_result_requirement: Admission is generally decided on the basis of the record already available at application time (which for a typical US 12th-grade applicant means grades through 11th grade plus first-semester 12th-grade grades submitted via Mid-Year Report), and remains contingent on the student's final senior-year transcript not showing a significant decline — a continued-satisfactory-performance condition, not a target-grade condition.

sources.note: Explains Mid-Year Report as the mechanism for updating admissions offices on senior-year performance
Harvard's own Common App Mid-Year Report form, illustrative of the actual (not predicted) grade-reporting mechanism

conditional_vs_unconditional_admission.concept_exists: Yes, but structurally different from the UK model. There is no US-wide standardized term equivalent to 'conditional offer' tied to a future target grade. Instead, the near-universal practice is that an admission decision is communicated as an acceptance, but that acceptance carries an implicit or explicit condition that the student's final high school record (via the Final Report / final transcript) must be 'consistent with' the record the offer was based on — i.e., no significant, unexplained decline.
conditional_vs_unconditional_admission.explanation: Mechanism: (1) Admission decision issued based on the record available at application time (through 11th grade, sometimes plus first-semester 12th-grade via Mid-Year Report). (2) Offer letters commonly include contingency language — illustrative quoted examples found in this research: Northwestern's stated letter language is 'contingent upon the successful completion of your senior year and a review of your final transcript'; University of South Florida's stated policy is 'all offers of admission are conditional, pending receipt of final transcripts showing work comparable in quality to that upon which the offer was based.' (3) After graduation, the school sends the Final Report/final transcript; the university reviews it, and in the large majority of cases simply confirms enrollment. (4) Outright rescission is uncommon but real — reporting compiled from admissions-consulting sources suggests roughly one-fifth of colleges report rescinding at least one admitted student's offer in a given year, usually triggered by a dramatic GPA decline, failing grades, failure to graduate, or disciplinary/integrity issues, rather than a modest single-grade dip. This 'rescission' framing, while a genuine and important structural feature, was sourced mainly through admissions-consulting compilations rather than a single authoritative government/NACAC dataset in this pass, so treat the specific statistic (~22%) as lower-confidence discovery-tier evidence, while the underlying mechanism (offers are conditional on maintaining performance, evidenced by illustrative real letter language from Northwestern and USF) is better supported.

subject_prerequisites.pattern: University/programme-level guidance, not a national or even system-wide hard rule. Competitive engineering, computer science, and pre-health programs commonly state an expectation (sometimes strongly worded, rarely a strict blocking prerequisite for admission itself) that applicants complete a rigorous math/science sequence — typically calculus and physics for engineering, biology/chemistry for pre-med tracks — 'available at their high school.' The emphasis is usually framed as 'take the most rigorous courses your school offers' rather than a fixed universal checklist, because US high schools vary enormously in what they offer, and admissions offices explicitly account for that variation.
illustrative_examples: Georgia Institute of Technology: admissions guidance states students should be prepared to begin college coursework in calculus, and that admissions officers look for applicants who challenged themselves with the most demanding math/science curriculum available at their high school (AP/IB/dual-enrollment/honors calculus, physics, chemistry, computer science).

MIT: admissions guidance (mitadmissions.org 'Preparing for MIT' page) states the expectation is exposure to at least the fundamentals of calculus before high school graduation and a rigorous math/science track, without mandating a single fixed national syllabus.

standardized_tests.mandatory_optional_status: Fragmented and university-specific — this is the single fastest-moving policy area in US admissions right now and must be verified per-university before advising any student. As of this research (retrieved 2026-08-20), reported patterns include: mandatory-testing reinstated at Harvard, Yale, Dartmouth, Brown, Cornell (Fall 2026 entry), the University of Pennsylvania, MIT, Caltech, and Stanford; Princeton and Columbia remain test-optional through the 2026-27 cycle but have each announced testing will become mandatory starting the 2027-28 cycle; the entire Florida and Georgia public university systems have reinstated mandatory testing; Auburn University is phasing to fully mandatory testing for Fall 2027; the University of Alabama will require a test score starting with the Fall 2027 entering class only for applicants with a cumulative high school GPA below 3.0 (a conditional/threshold policy, university-level); Notre Dame, Duke, Northwestern remain test-optional for the 2026-27 cycle, and Vanderbilt has stated it will remain test-optional through Fall 2027 and Fall 2028 entry.
standardized_tests.current_cycle_note: IMPORTANT CONFIDENCE CAVEAT: the specific institution-by-institution claims above were sourced from admissions-consulting/test-prep aggregator sites (College Transitions, The College Investor, Aralia Education, IvyMax, Carnegie Prep, Oriel Admissions, Principia Education, PathIvy), which the research brief's own source-priority rules class as discovery-tier, not foundational evidence. No single official government or NACAC dataset consolidating current-cycle testing policy across universities was found in this pass. Every specific university's testing requirement should be re-verified directly against that university's own admissions website (priority-3 source) before being used in real counselor advice to a student, and refreshed periodically given how fast this landscape is moving (multiple reversals occurred within 2024-2026 alone).
standardized_tests.academic_cycle: 2026-27 admission cycle (Fall 2027 entry), as of retrieval date 2026-08-20; several universities have already announced 2027-28-cycle changes distinct from their current 2026-27 policy — cycle must always be specified when stating a testing policy.
standardized_tests.ap_exam_role_in_admissions_vs_credit: Per College Board's own AP Students site: colleges weigh many more factors than the AP exam score itself when making admission decisions, including the rigor of the course taken and the school-reported course grade; students are advised to check each target college's own admissions site to see whether sending official AP scores will 'help support' the application (implying it is a supplementary/optional signal for many schools, not a mandatory input). By contrast, official AP score reports are typically sent to colleges AFTER admission specifically to be evaluated for college credit or course placement — a distinct, post-enrollment process from the admissions decision itself. This directly supports treating 'the AP course + its school grade' (rigor signal, pre-enrollment, admissions-relevant) and 'the AP exam numeric score' (credit/placement, largely post-enrollment) as two different data points in ORYN's model, matching the research brief's own framing.

language_requirements.framework: No single national English-proficiency test is mandated. Universities individually decide which tests they accept — commonly TOEFL iBT (including the Home Edition), IELTS Academic (including IELTS Online), Duolingo English Test, and in some cases specific Cambridge English Scale tests — and set their own minimum score thresholds.
language_requirements.exemption_pattern: A common (but university-set, not national) exemption pattern has two branches: (1) citizenship/nativity-based exemption for applicants from countries where English is a primary official language (patterns found include Australia, Canada outside Quebec, the UK, Ireland, New Zealand, Guyana, and some Anglophone African/Caribbean countries — the exact country list is university-specific); and (2) an English-medium-of-instruction exemption for applicants who completed a substantial portion of schooling (commonly framed as 3+ years, sometimes framed as the entirety of secondary school) in English as the primary language of instruction, verified via school records/transcripts rather than a separate test. Per the University of Pennsylvania's own official FAQ, exemptions of this kind exist but are 'not guaranteed' and 'not automatic in most cases' — i.e., the applicant typically must actively request/demonstrate the exemption rather than assume it applies.
language_requirements.where_variation_begins: The specific accepted tests, the specific minimum required scores, and the exact exemption criteria (years required, automatic vs. request-based, which countries qualify) are all university-level decisions — there is no national baseline score or national exemption rule.

application_timing.cycle: 2026-27 admission cycle (applications submitted during the 2026-27 school year for Fall 2027 entry). Common App's 2026-27 season officially opened July 31, 2026.
application_timing.major_deadline_pattern: Early rounds (Early Decision / Early Action / Restrictive Early Action) cluster around early-to-mid November (commonly November 1 or November 15, university-set); Regular Decision deadlines cluster around January 1 to January 15 (also university-set); Rolling Admission has no single fixed deadline — applications are reviewed continuously as received, typically from a stated opening date until either a stated final deadline or until available spots fill. These clustering dates are an industry-wide convention reinforced by Common App's own aggregate reporting cadence (Common App itself publishes cycle-tracking reports at the 'through Nov 1' and 'through Jan 1' checkpoints), but each individual university still sets its own exact deadline date — this is a platform-reinforced convention, not a national rule.
application_timing.early_deadlines: Typically ~November 1–15 for ED/EA/REA/ED I; some universities additionally offer an 'ED II' round with a January deadline (functionally a second, later binding round) — ED II specifics are university-level, not universal.
application_timing.regular_deadlines: Typically January 1–15 for Regular Decision at most Common App/Coalition member institutions that use a fixed RD deadline; some universities use Rolling Admission instead of a fixed RD deadline.

sources.note: Common App's own official cycle-tracking report using Nov 1 / Jan 1 as standard checkpoints (from the prior 2025-26 cycle, illustrating the platform's standard reporting cadence)
College Board's own explanation of ED/EA mechanics and October SAT deadline implications

constraints: Early Decision (ED) is binding: per College Board's own counselor guidance, a student accepted ED 'must attend the college,' may 'apply to only one college early decision,' and must 'withdraw all other applications if accepted' — a real, structural, single-choice commitment.

Restrictive/Single-Choice Early Action (REA), per Common App's own admission-plan definitions, is non-binding on enrollment but can still restrict the applicant from simultaneously applying ED or EA (or REA) to other colleges during that same early round — the exact restriction terms are set by each university offering REA, not standardized nationally.
Early Action (regular, non-restrictive) and Rolling Admission carry no binding-commitment or apply-elsewhere restriction.

Common App itself caps a single account at 20 colleges (platform-level constraint, not a legal cap); applying to more requires using an additional platform (Coalition/Scoir, a state system, or direct institutional application).
application_strategy_constraints.explanation: The practically significant counselor-relevant constraint is ED's binding nature: a student who applies ED to School A cannot simultaneously apply ED (or, at many schools, EA/REA) elsewhere, and if admitted must withdraw all other pending applications and enroll — meaning an ED choice forecloses comparison-shopping on financial aid offers from other schools, which is a real strategic and financial trade-off a counselor should surface explicitly, not just an academic one.
