Swiss ENIC (hosted at swissuniversities, Bern) is the national ENIC-NARIC contact point, but its documented remit is evaluating foreign higher-education (tertiary) degrees for comparability via a non-binding 'statement of comparability' -- it is not the mechanism governing upper-secondary diploma recognition for Bachelor's entry; that role sits with the swissuniversities country list plus each university's own admissions office.
B_qualification_eligibility.baseline_qualification_expectation: CDIP's 2011 and 2015 declarations commit to long-term exam-free university access for gymnasiale Maturitat holders, confirmed directly by ETH Zurich: 'If you hold a Swiss Matura, you gain direct admission to any ETH bachelor's programme -- no entrance exam required.' For foreign diplomas, direct exam-free admission requires meeting a specific documented threshold -- e.g. IB Diploma 38/42 points (without bonus points) with a defined Higher/Standard Level subject spread; German Abitur, Austrian Reifeprufung, or French Baccalaureat with a minimum grade average of roughly 70% across three core examined subjects (mathematics; physics, chemistry or biology; language of instruction or a foreign language) plus four more subjects studied in the final three years, and, for France specifically, an overall 'moyenne finale' of 16.00/20 or above.
B_qualification_eligibility.subject_prerequisites_general: ETH Zurich's official country-by-country admission requirements document reveals a recurring shared template applied almost uniformly across roughly 190 countries: the applicant's final 2-3 years of schooling must show mathematics, a science (physics/chemistry/biology), and the language of instruction or a foreign language as examined subjects, plus four further subjects studied (not necessarily examined) in the final three years of schooling. Only the named certificate and the specific grade threshold vary by country; this 3-core-plus-4-more structure itself does not.
B_qualification_eligibility.equivalency_process: Each university maintains its own admission regulations built on the shared swissuniversities country list, revised annually and stated to apply 'exclusively to the year of study indicated.' Country-specific certificate names, subject requirements, and grade thresholds are published per country; where the documented bar is not met, ETHZ's Comprehensive Entrance Examination (or EPFL's own entrance exam, open to applicants from non-EU/EFTA/UK countries) is the fallback.
B_qualification_eligibility.university_discretion: Substantial, and structurally different from every other country in this package: even where the shared swissuniversities baseline is met, ETH Zurich and EPFL each add their own additional entrance-exam layer that the 10 cantonal universities do not require, and the University of St. Gallen adds a quota-driven selection procedure for all foreign-certificate holders regardless of qualification strength. The same input qualification can therefore be sufficient at one university and require an additional exam or selection procedure at another.

credentials_covered.turkiye_meb: Only Anadolu Lisesi Diplomasi and Fen Lisesi Diplomasi are named as recognized on swissuniversities' list and, verbatim, in ETH Zurich's own official PDF. See the dedicated Turkiye section below.
credentials_covered.ib_diploma: Direct exam-free admission at ETHZ with 38/42 points (without bonus points), specific Higher Level subjects (Mathematics: applications and interpretation, or analysis and approaches; plus physics, chemistry or biology; plus one language A) and three further Standard Level subjects from a defined list. Otherwise, ETHZ's Reduced Entrance Examination applies.
credentials_covered.a_levels: Great Britain track: (I)GCE with three Advanced Levels (or Cambridge Pre-U) in mathematics, a science, and the language of instruction/a foreign language, grade A in each (Pre-U: D3), plus at least four additional (I)GCE AS/(I)GCSE or Pre-U Short Course subjects, for exam-free ETHZ admission; otherwise ETHZ's Reduced Entrance Examination applies. Scotland has its own parallel Advanced Higher-based pathway with the same structure.
credentials_covered.ap_plus_us_diploma: Not independently confirmed in this research pass for Switzerland specifically; expected by pattern (per the general foreign-diploma template) to require the US diploma plus a qualifying combination of AP exam scores to reach a direct- admission threshold, otherwise gated behind an entrance exam -- flagged as an inference from the general template, not a confirmed US-specific finding.
credentials_covered.french_bac: Baccalaureat general with proof of Specialite mathematiques/mathematiques expertes, Specialite sciences de la vie et de la terre or physique-chimie, and the language of instruction/premiere langue vivante during the final two years, each passed at a minimum 70% (14.00/20) average, plus four more subjects studied, AND an overall 'moyenne finale' of 16.00/20 or above, for exam-free ETHZ admission; otherwise ETHZ's Reduced Entrance Examination applies.
credentials_covered.german_abitur: Zeugnis der allgemeinen Hochschulreife with the same three-core-subject (mathematics; physics/chemistry/biology; language) 70% average pattern plus four more subjects, for exam-free ETHZ admission (Pharmaceutical Sciences and Architecture additionally require a certificate of university admission from a recognised German university); otherwise ETHZ's Reduced Entrance Examination applies.

B_qualification_eligibility.scope: national/joint-federal-cantonal (Matura recognition) / platform-coordination (swissuniversities' non-binding country list) / university (binding admission decision and any additional entrance-exam or selection-procedure layer)

turkiye_applicant_view.standard_diploma_sufficient_for_direct_e: Not sufficient on its own anywhere. Only Anadolu Lisesi Diplomasi and Fen Lisesi Diplomasi are named as recognized upper-secondary certificates for Turkey (Lisbon Convention signatory, marked '(L)') -- other MEB-system Lise sub-types (Genel Lise, Meslek Lisesi, Imam-Hatip Lisesi) are simply not named on swissuniversities' list or ETH's own PDF, a genuine gap rather than a confirmed exclusion. At the 10 non-ETH/EPFL universities, the named diploma plus a separate 'certificate of university admission to a 4-year programme in the desired academic subject provided by a recognised Turkish university' is stated as sufficient, with no further ECUS or entrance exam. At ETH Zurich specifically, confirmed verbatim in ETH's own official PDF (Academic Year 2025/26): even the diploma plus that Turkish-university-admission certificate still requires ETHZ's Reduced Entrance Examination; without the certificate, the Comprehensive Entrance Examination applies. There is no exam-free pathway for this qualification type at ETHZ. At EPFL, Turkey falls under 'a country that is not a member of EU, EFTA, nor UK,' making the applicant eligible for EPFL's own entrance exam (in French). St. Gallen additionally requires all foreign-certificate holders, Turkish applicants included, to pass its own foreign-quota selection procedure regardless of diploma type. USI adds unspecified 'special conditions' (Admission Regulations art. 8 para. 3).
turkiye_applicant_view.additional_qualifications_commonly_requi: A certificate of university admission to a 4-year programme in the desired academic subject, issued by a recognised Turkish university, is the most consistently-documented additional requirement (required at the 10 non-ETH/EPFL universities as a sufficient supplement; effectively also relevant to ETHZ's Reduced-vs-Comprehensive exam distinction). ECUS was confirmed as not applicable to Turkey specifically, since Turkey is a Lisbon Convention signatory.
turkiye_applicant_view.ap_ib_a_level_impact: Materially changes the picture. A Turkish-school student who also holds a full IB Diploma (38/42 points with the defined Higher/Standard Level subject pattern) or A-Levels (three subjects at grade A in mathematics, a science and a language, plus four further subjects) is evaluated under those criteria instead of the plain-Lise criteria, and can reach ETH Zurich's exam-free direct-admission bar -- a materially easier route than the plain-Lise-plus-Turkish-university-admission-certificate pathway, which still requires at least the Reduced Entrance Examination at ETHZ.
turkiye_applicant_view.national_entrance_exam_relevance: No Swiss source names YKS (the Turkish national university entrance exam) directly or sets a YKS score threshold. What is explicitly required instead, at most Swiss universities, is proof of admission to a Turkish university's own 4-year programme -- and since admission to Turkish Lisans programmes is itself YKS-gated, YKS functions as the mechanism that produces the required certificate, even though it is never cited by name. This is an inferred structural/causal link, not a Swiss-source-confirmed criterion, and is a genuine gap the same way YKS's role in Dutch VWO-equivalence was flagged as unresolved in the Netherlands research.
turkiye_applicant_view.foundation_year_common: No dedicated official Swiss government 'foundation year' pathway for foreign qualifications generally was identified in this pass (distinct from Germany's Studienkolleg). A secondary-sourced (not ethz.ch-primary-confirmed) claim describes ETH Zurich individually evaluating one completed year of accredited home-country university study as a transfer-admission alternative -- flag as secondary-corroborated only, not verbatim-confirmed, and not established as a general Swiss system feature beyond this one specific, unconfirmed ETHZ claim.
turkiye_applicant_view.recognition_centralized_or_university_sp: Mixed, but tilted toward university-specific in the outcome that matters to a student -- more sharply than in the Netherlands. swissuniversities supplies the underlying shared, non-binding country-level comparison (which two Turkish certificate types are named as recognized, and what supplementary certificate is generally expected), but each university then applies its own binding rule on top: 10 cantonal universities treat the diploma-plus-certificate combination as sufficient outright; ETH Zurich requires its own Reduced or Comprehensive Entrance Examination regardless; EPFL requires its own separate entrance exam; St. Gallen requires its foreign-quota selection procedure regardless of any of the above. A Turkish applicant cannot assume one university's requirements transfer to another.

academic_evidence_used.transcript_role: Full secondary-school transcript and the final school-leaving certificate are required as supporting evidence for the qualification-recognition assessment at every institution reviewed.
academic_evidence_used.native_grades_handling: Native grades are read on their original scale with country-specific minimum thresholds set by each university (e.g. the recurring ~70% average across core subjects seen throughout ETH's country-by-country PDF), not force-converted to a universal GPA -- the same pattern already found in every other country in this package.
academic_evidence_used.predicted_grades_role: See the dedicated predicted_grades section. No native Swiss-Matura predicted-grade artifact exists; foreign IB/A-Level/AP predicted or interim grades are submitted and relied on operationally by at least one university (St. Gallen) pending final results.
academic_evidence_used.final_grades_role: Final results are ultimately required; St. Gallen's own process explicitly permits submitting the final certificate 'as soon as you receive it, no later than the start of the course' if it is not yet available at application time.
academic_evidence_used.external_exams_role: For gymnasiale Maturitat holders themselves, the Matura is awarded on continuous assessment plus final cantonal examinations, with an overall average of at least 4.0/6.0 required and an interdisciplinary matura thesis (at least 60 pages, orally defended). For foreign applicants, whatever externally-set exams are part of their own curriculum are treated as already encoded within the home-country diploma, evaluated via the swissuniversities/university equivalence process rather than a separate Swiss external-exam layer.
academic_evidence_used.course_rigor_signal: Read through the recurring ETH-documented subject-breadth template (mathematics, a science, and the language of instruction as examined subjects, plus four more studied subjects) rather than a programme-specific subject-mapping mechanism like the Netherlands' profielen.
academic_evidence_used.subject_prerequisites: See the dedicated subject_prerequisites section -- for foreign qualifications, subject coverage is built directly into the recognition template itself rather than layered on afterward; for Swiss-Matura holders, whether individual programmes require a specific Matura Schwerpunktfach was not independently confirmed this pass.
academic_evidence_used.standardized_tests: No SAT/ACT-style general requirement. See the dedicated standardized_tests section for EMS (Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary Medicine/Chiropractic) and the ETHZ/EPFL/HSG university-specific instruments.

predicted_grades.are_used: Not as a native Swiss-Matura concept. Cantonal gymnasiale Matura final exams commonly sit in May-June, after the ~30 April general application deadline several universities cite, meaning Swiss-track applicants, like foreign ones, may plausibly apply before their own final results are confirmed -- but no source reviewed explicitly labels this 'conditional admission' at a system level the way the UK or Netherlands do. Treat as a structurally plausible but unconfirmed inference, a genuine gap, not a verified finding.
predicted_grades.where: Predicted or interim grades as an artifact are used where an applicant's own foreign curriculum natively produces them (IB predicted grades; UK A-Level predicted grades) -- confirmed operationally at the University of St. Gallen, whose own checklist explicitly allows submitting 'the half-year report of the final year' or a school confirmation with all subjects in the final year if the final certificate isn't yet available.
predicted_grades.by_whom: For IB/A-Level applicants: issued by the applicant's own school/teachers under IB or exam-board rules, not generated by any Swiss body. For native Matura-track applicants: not applicable in the confirmed sources -- no Swiss-issued 'predicted grade' document was identified.
predicted_grades.for_what: To let a university provisionally process an application before final results are known, given that several application windows (e.g. St. Gallen's 1 October-30 April) close well before IB/A-Level or, plausibly, Swiss cantonal Matura final results are confirmed.
predicted_grades.conditional_offer_relationship: Narrower and less formally named than in the Netherlands or UK -- see the dedicated conditional_vs_unconditional_admission section. The functional equivalent is administrative: interim documents accepted provisionally, final certificate required before the programme starts, without a distinctly-named 'conditional offer' status.
predicted_grades.final_result_requirement: Yes -- confirmed directly at St. Gallen: the final certificate must be submitted 'as soon as you receive it, no later than the start of the course.'
predicted_grades.scope: university (St. Gallen confirmed directly; not independently verified as a uniform national practice)

conditional_vs_unconditional_admission.concept_exists: In a narrower, more procedural sense than the UK or Netherlands, plus a clearer two-stage sense specifically for restricted fields.
conditional_vs_unconditional_admission.explanation: No source reviewed uses a distinctly-named 'conditional offer' status or artifact (no equivalent of UCAS Track or Dutch voorwaardelijke toelating) for the general admissions route -- the functional equivalent is administrative: interim documents (e.g. a half-year report) are accepted provisionally, and the final certificate must be submitted before the programme starts. This places Switzerland closer to Germany's and Italy's 'narrow procedural sense' cluster than the UK/Netherlands' 'load-bearing mechanic' cluster. Restricted fields show a clearer two-stage decoupling instead: for Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary Medicine/Chiropractic, holding a Matura-equivalent qualification establishes eligibility only; actual admission depends separately on the EMS ranking (or, in French-speaking Switzerland, the first-year selection exam) -- eligible and admitted are explicitly different states for these fields, structurally similar to the Netherlands' numerus fixus 'selection-conditional' concept.

subject_prerequisites.pattern: For foreign qualifications, subject prerequisites are built directly into the qualification-recognition template itself (mathematics, a science, and the language of instruction as examined subjects, plus four more studied subjects), not layered on as a separate programme-specific filter the way the Netherlands' profielen operate. For Swiss-Matura holders, whether individual Bachelor's programmes require a specific Matura Schwerpunktfach (subject specialization) was not independently confirmed in this research pass -- a genuine gap, unlike the Netherlands' well-documented VWO-profiel mapping.
subject_prerequisites.scope: national-template (foreign-qualification recognition) / programme (added content for specific restricted fields) / unconfirmed (Swiss-Matura programme-level requirements)
illustrative_examples: The recurring foreign-qualification template requires mathematics, physics/chemistry/biology, and the language of instruction as examined subjects (commonly at a ~70% average), plus four more subjects (from a list including computer science, geography, history, economics, another language) studied in the final three years of schooling.

EMS content (Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary Medicine/Chiropractic) tests scientific reasoning, spatial and quantitative ability, and memory/concentration rather than memorized biology, per swissuniversities' own EMS materials.
The University of Basel lists 'special provisions' for Sport, Exercise and Health alongside Medicine, Clinical Medicine and Dental Medicine.

standardized_tests.mandatory_optional_status: No SAT/ACT-style general requirement exists anywhere in the Swiss system, for domestic or international applicants. The dominant standardized instrument is EMS (Eignungstest fur das Medizinstudium), a full-day aptitude test (scientific reasoning, spatial and quantitative ability, memory/concentration -- not memorized biology) required by Basel, Bern, Fribourg, Zurich (incl. its Lucerne and St. Gallen tracks), USI and ETH Zurich for Human Medicine, Dentistry, Veterinary Medicine and Chiropractic. Per swissuniversities, EMS activates specifically 'when the number of study-interested persons exceeds the number of available study places by more than 20 percent.' Geneva, Lausanne and Neuchatel (French-speaking) do not use EMS at all -- confirmed by their absence from swissuniversities' own list of EMS-using institutions; secondary Swiss-press sourcing indicates they instead admit broadly into first-year Medicine (BMed1) and apply a competitive first-year/propaedeutic exam to determine progression to year two, a post-entry rather than pre-entry mechanism for the same restricted field.
standardized_tests.current_cycle_note: No evidence found of EMS's mechanism changing for the 2026-27 cycle. EPFL's new capacity-cap policy (see restricted_selective_programmes) is itself a genuine, recent (2025) change and should be re-verified each cycle through 2029.
programme_specific_tests: EMS -- full-day, ~CHF 300, once yearly (early July), used by the Basel/Bern/Fribourg/Zurich(+Lucerne/St.Gallen)/USI/ETH Zurich consortium for Medicine, Dentistry, Veterinary Medicine and Chiropractic; a single sitting is usable across the entire consortium.

ETH Zurich's own Reduced Entrance Examination (mathematics + one further subject) or Comprehensive Entrance Examination (mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, a language), conducted in German, for foreign diplomas not meeting the direct-admission threshold; CHF 550 / CHF 800.

EPFL's own entrance exam (French), open to holders of a Swiss maturite professionnelle/specialisee or an upper-secondary certificate from a non-EU/EFTA/UK country; CHF 150 registration tax + CHF 550/800 exam fee; passing the CMS preparatory mathematics course is an accepted equivalent alternative.

University of St. Gallen's online aptitude test (quantitative problem-solving + diagram/table interpretation, 70 minutes) plus a recorded video interview, used only within its foreign-applicant selection procedure (see restricted_selective_programmes), not a general admissions test.

language_requirements.framework: The most distinctive Swiss finding relative to every other country in this package: Bachelor's-level instruction is overwhelmingly in German, French or Italian, not English. ETH Zurich's Bachelor's programmes are taught in German from year one, 'mostly German' thereafter with only some individual English courses; EPFL's own documents and registration are conducted in French; Geneva/Lausanne/Neuchatel are French-medium; USI is Italian-medium. Required proficiency in the instruction language is commonly C1 CEFR (UZH and Bern require German C1; St. Gallen recommends C1), while Geneva requires French at a B2 level (DELF/DALF or UNIGE's own test) for non-French-medium applicants. IELTS/TOEFL-style English proficiency is not the load-bearing language gate for most Swiss Bachelor's programmes -- a materially different structural emphasis than the Netherlands, UK, or Germany's English-taught tracks, and a genuine contrast with Swiss Master's programmes, which are commonly English.
language_requirements.exemption_pattern: Not independently confirmed in detail this pass beyond the general expectation (consistent with other countries in this package) that prior education substantially conducted in the instruction language, or being a national of a country where that language is official, would typically exempt an applicant from a separate proficiency test -- flagged as an inference from pattern, not a Switzerland-specific confirmed rule.
language_requirements.where_variation_begins: At the university/programme level, and additionally at the whole-institution level by choice of linguistic region (German-medium vs. French-medium vs. Italian-medium universities) -- a genuinely different variation axis from every other country researched. A confirmed exception to the German/French/Italian pattern exists at the University of St. Gallen: its Assessment Year (Bachelor year one) in Economic Sciences (Business Administration, Economics, International Affairs, and Law and Economics) 'can be taken either entirely in English or entirely in German' (HSG's own official page), though the standalone Law Assessment Year and the Computer Science Assessment Year at HSG are German-only.

application_timing.cycle: 2025-2026 / 2026-2027 academic years, cited alongside registration mechanics that structurally repeat each year; re-verify exact dates closer to any future cycle.
application_timing.major_deadline_pattern: No single national deadline exists. A general (non-restricted-programme) deadline around 30 April is cited across several universities; the University of St. Gallen's own official page independently confirms an application window of 1 October-30 April for its Assessment Year (autumn-semester start only).
application_timing.numerus_fixus_deadline: Not a single shared date -- each restricted-field mechanism has its own separate timing. EMS sits once yearly, in early July, on its own registration schedule not independently confirmed to the day this pass. EPFL's own entrance-exam registration runs 1 October-1 December for a January scientific-exam sitting, distinct from EPFL's general application timeline. ETH's own entrance examination sits annually in 'the third and fourth weeks of the year' (mid/late January). St. Gallen's foreign-applicant selection procedure runs on two fixed annual sitting windows (February and June).
application_timing.visa_driven_practical_deadline: Non-EU/EFTA applicants who need a Swiss student visa are commonly advised (secondary-corroborated) to submit their university application by roughly end-February, to leave enough time for visa processing -- explicitly a visa-processing-driven practical target, not a university-set admissions deadline, and the two should not be conflated.

constraints: No shared platform means no shared numeric choice-limit -- unlike UCAS's 5, the Netherlands' 2-numerus-fixus cap, or Germany's 12-preference hochschulstart list, a student may apply directly to as many of the 12 institutions as time and money allow.
Application fees apply per institution: commonly CHF 100-250, rising to CHF 268 at St. Gallen from autumn 2026.
EMS is a partial exception to the 'no shared mechanism' pattern -- one sitting is usable across the entire EMS consortium.

EPFL's new 2025-2029 admissions cap (3,000 first-year Bachelor's places, for at least four years) is a live, time-bound constraint: Swiss nationals, Swiss Matura holders, and all CMS/entrance-exam passers are guaranteed a place, while EPFL's own announcement separately states non-Swiss-qualification holders 'compete' on secondary-school GPA/points if the cap is oversubscribed.
St. Gallen's 25%-by-law foreign-student quota plus its twice-yearly-only, two-stage selection procedure is a further hard constraint specific to foreign-certificate holders targeting HSG.
application_strategy_constraints.explanation: Exactly which applicant subgroup EPFL's GPA-ranking mechanism touches (direct-admission foreign-diploma holders specifically, versus all non-Swiss-certificate holders generally) was not fully disambiguated in the source reviewed and should not be over-specified in ORYN's logic without further confirmation from EPFL directly.

personal_statement_essays.role: Not a standard requirement anywhere in the general admissions route reviewed. The closest analogue is the University of St. Gallen's foreign-applicant-only selection procedure, which includes a roughly 10-minute recorded video interview on motivation and interests -- oral/recorded rather than written, and specific to HSG's foreign quota rather than a general Swiss feature.
personal_statement_essays.explanation: An aggregator-sourced claim that the University of Geneva requires a statement of purpose, letters of recommendation and a CV was not corroborated on UNIGE's own official admissions page (which lists only diploma, grade, language and ECUS-type requirements) and should be treated as unconfirmed generic aggregator content, not a verified Geneva-specific requirement -- an explicit example of why secondary sites may be used only to discover candidate primary sources, never as the basis for a claim.

recommendation_letters.role: Not identified as a standard requirement in any official Swiss source reviewed for Bachelor's admission.
recommendation_letters.explanation: Consistent with the pattern already established across the Netherlands, Germany, and Italy in this package -- recommendation letters simply do not appear as a structural requirement in a threshold/qualification-based or aptitude-test-based admissions model.

extracurricular_activities.role: Not a documented factor in any official source reviewed for the general admission route -- the threshold/qualification-based model (or, for restricted fields, the aptitude-test/ranking model) leaves no structural place for a holistic activities review.
extracurricular_activities.nuance: The same pattern already confirmed for Italy and, for non-selective programmes, the Netherlands. No evidence was found of extracurricular activity entering even indirectly (e.g. via a motivation letter) for the general Swiss route, since a written motivation letter is not itself a standard general requirement here.

interviews_tests_portfolios.pattern: Four distinct, non-overlapping mechanisms confirmed: (1) University of St. Gallen's recorded video interview, foreign-quota applicants only; (2) the EMS aptitude test, for Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary Medicine/Chiropractic in most linguistic regions; (3) ETH Zurich's and EPFL's own bespoke entrance examinations, for foreign diplomas that don't clear the direct-admission bar; (4) Geneva/Lausanne/Neuchatel's post-entry first-year selection exam for Medicine, structurally distinct from EMS.
interviews_tests_portfolios.when_applicable: Only for foreign-certificate holders at St. Gallen, for restricted-field applicants (Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary Medicine/Chiropractic), or for foreign-diploma holders at ETHZ/EPFL who don't meet the direct-admission threshold. Not applicable to Swiss-Matura holders in non-restricted fields. Portfolio-based Bachelor's admission (art/design/music) was not independently confirmed in this research pass -- such programmes exist in Switzerland (commonly at Fachhochschule/HES level, e.g. Zurich University of the Arts) but fell outside this pass's scope; a genuine gap, not a confirmed absence.

restricted_selective_programmes.restriction_mechanisms_explanation: At least four structurally distinct mechanisms operate simultaneously -- Swiss 'numerus clausus' is not one system. (1) EMS pre-entry test: Basel, Bern, Fribourg, Zurich (+ Lucerne/St. Gallen tracks), USI, ETH Zurich, for Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary Medicine/Chiropractic, activated when demand exceeds places by more than 20%. (2) French-region post-entry selection: Geneva, Lausanne, Neuchatel admit broadly into first-year Medicine, then rank/cut after first-year exams -- the same restricted fields, a genuinely different mechanism, split by linguistic region rather than by programme or university choice as elsewhere in this package. (3) EPFL's blanket capacity cap (3,000 first-year Bachelor's places at EPFL specifically, 2025-2029): not field-specific -- caps EPFL's entire Bachelor's intake, with Swiss-qualification and exam-route holders guaranteed and other applicants potentially GPA-ranked. (4) St. Gallen's 25%-by-law foreign-student quota, confirmed directly on HSG's own official page ('Foreign applicants with a recognised international educational certificate can only be admitted through the HSG selection procedure... the number of places for foreign applicants... is limited by law') -- gated by certificate origin/nationality across all HSG fields, not by academic field at all. (5) Narrower programme-specific caps also exist, e.g. Basel's 'special provisions' for Sport, Exercise and Health.
restricted_selective_programmes.current_mechanism: As of the 2026-27 cycle, this is a genuinely plural, not a single, system, and the EPFL capacity cap specifically is a recent (2025) and time-bound (through at least 2029) policy change that should be re-verified each future cycle rather than treated as a permanent fixture.
example_fields: Human Medicine, Dentistry, Veterinary Medicine, Chiropractic (EMS-track institutions)
Human Medicine at Geneva, Lausanne, Neuchatel (French-region post-entry track)
All Bachelor's fields at EPFL (2025-2029 blanket capacity cap)
All fields at the University of St. Gallen for foreign-certificate holders specifically (25% quota)
Sport, Exercise and Health at the University of Basel

admissions_decision_model.dominant_model: Multi-tier, with a foreign-vs-Swiss-qualification axis baked in even at the 'ordinary' level -- more finely stratified than any other country in this package.
admissions_decision_model.explanation: (a) Swiss Matura + non-restricted field: threshold-based, essentially automatic. (b) Foreign diploma meeting a direct-admission grade/subject threshold (IB 38+, Abitur/Bac ~70%+16/20, etc.): also threshold-based and exam-free. (c) Foreign diploma not meeting that bar: threshold-based but gated behind a pass/fail university entrance exam (not a ranked competition) at the 10 cantonal universities -- except that EPFL's new capacity cap can convert this into a genuinely ranked/competitive step in an oversubscribed cycle. (d) Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary Medicine/Chiropractic: genuinely selection/ranking-based (EMS score, or the French-region first-year rank). (e) University of St. Gallen: genuinely selection/ranking-based for all foreign-qualification applicants regardless of field, because of the 25% legal quota. No disclosed percentage-weighted formula was found anywhere in this system.

safe_inferences: It is safe to infer that a Swiss-Matura holder targeting a non-restricted field can be treated as essentially certain of admission once the Matura is confirmed.

It is safe to infer that a foreign applicant whose diploma clears the swissuniversities/ETH direct-admission threshold (specific IB points/subjects, or ~70%+ Abitur/Bac-style average with matching subjects) can be treated as exam-free eligible at most institutions.

It is safe to infer that a Turkish MEB-system applicant holding only a plain Lise diploma (i.e. not Anadolu Lisesi or Fen Lisesi) should be flagged as an unconfirmed-recognition case requiring direct university verification, not assumed eligible.

It is safe to infer that any Turkish applicant should be told a Turkish-university admission certificate is very likely also required, and that ETH Zurich requires its Reduced Entrance Examination regardless of whether that certificate is produced.

It is safe to infer that any applicant targeting Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary Medicine/Chiropractic must be told which linguistic-region mechanism (EMS vs. French-region first-year exam) applies to their target universities, since these are not interchangeable.
It is safe to infer that recommendation letters and broad extracurricular review are not meaningful admissions levers anywhere in this system.
unsafe_inferences: It is unsafe to assume Switzerland has any shared application platform, even a registration-only one -- it does not.

It is unsafe to assume swissuniversities' country list accepting a diploma type means admission is secured -- it establishes eligibility at most, and ETHZ/EPFL commonly add their own entrance-exam layer on top even then.

It is unsafe to assume 'numerus clausus' is one national mechanism in Switzerland -- EMS, the French-region first-year exam, EPFL's new blanket cap, and St. Gallen's foreign quota are four different things with different triggers.

It is unsafe to assume Swiss Bachelor's programmes are commonly English-taught by analogy with Swiss Master's programmes or with the Netherlands/Germany -- outside a small number of specific tracks (confirmed at HSG), they are not.

It is unsafe to assume a YKS score is itself a named Swiss admission criterion -- only the resulting Turkish-university admission certificate is named; the YKS linkage is inferred, not source-confirmed.
It is unsafe to assume the 'one year of completed foreign university study' ETH transfer route is verbatim-confirmed -- it is secondary-sourced only in this pass.
It is unsafe to assume EPFL's new capacity cap is permanent -- it is explicitly framed as a 2025-2029, at-least-four-year measure, reviewable afterward.

eligibility_competitiveness_fit.eligibility: An objective, checkable threshold for the large majority of the system: is the qualification Matura-equivalent (per the Swiss-Matura route or the swissuniversities-documented foreign-diploma route), and, where applicable, has the required entrance exam been passed.
eligibility_competitiveness_fit.competitiveness: Essentially does not exist as a separate concept for Swiss-Matura holders in non-restricted fields, or for foreign applicants who clear a direct-admission threshold -- eligible and admitted are the same outcome, similar to the Netherlands' and Italy's non-selective programmes. It re-emerges sharply and becomes dominant in exactly the same places restriction applies: Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary Medicine/Chiropractic (via EMS ranking or the French-region first-year exam), EPFL once its new capacity cap binds, and St. Gallen for every foreign applicant regardless of field.
eligibility_competitiveness_fit.fit: Has essentially no formal role anywhere in the system reviewed -- no motivation letter, personal statement, or holistic review exists for the general route; the closest the system comes is St. Gallen's foreign-quota video interview, which assesses motivation as one structured input rather than a freestanding narrative judgment.

counselor_actions: Confirm which of the 12 institutions a target programme sits at, since each runs a fully separate application with no shared platform to lean on.

For any foreign-qualification student, check the swissuniversities country list first, but never treat listing on it as equivalent to admission -- verify per-university whether an entrance exam (ETHZ/EPFL) or a selection procedure (St. Gallen) applies on top.

For a Turkish MEB-educated student: confirm whether the diploma is Anadolu Lisesi or Fen Lisesi (the only named types); arrange proof of admission to a Turkish university programme in the matching subject proactively, since most Swiss universities require it; and set expectations for ETH Zurich/EPFL specifically, where an entrance exam applies regardless of that documentation.
Where the student holds AP/IB/A-Levels alongside a Turkish diploma, evaluate under those criteria instead, since they can reach an exam-free bar the plain-Lise pathway cannot.

For any Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary Medicine/Chiropractic target, determine early which linguistic-region mechanism applies -- EMS requires dedicated aptitude-test preparation months ahead; the French-region route instead demands a strong first university year.

For EPFL, do not assume a guaranteed place for a non-Swiss-qualification applicant even after clearing the entrance-exam pathway, given the 2025-2029 capacity cap -- monitor EPFL's own communications each cycle.

For any St. Gallen (HSG) target, budget for the mandatory two-stage foreign-applicant selection procedure (fixed February or June sittings) well in advance, since it cannot be bypassed by qualification strength alone.

Confirm the actual language of instruction per programme -- do not assume English is available anywhere outside the confirmed HSG Economic Sciences exception, and plan German/French/Italian proficiency (commonly C1) accordingly, well before application.

data_model_implications.notes: Switzerland requires ORYN's data model to represent admission facts across at least five distinct scope levels, more than any other country in this package: (1) joint federal-cantonal (Matura recognition itself, via MAR/MAV), (2) inter-cantonal coordination (CDIP's exam-free-access commitment; swissuniversities' shared but non-binding country list), (3) federal-institution-specific (ETHZ's and EPFL's own entrance-exam rules and EPFL's new capacity cap, applying only to these two federally-run institutions and nowhere else), (4) cantonal-university-specific (each of the 10 cantonal universities' own admission regulations, including St. Gallen's quota-driven selection procedure), and (5) linguistic-region clustering as an independent axis cutting across university boundaries (the EMS-vs-French-region-exam split for identical restricted fields). A single 'country requirement' record per qualification type would be actively misleading here -- arguably more so than for any other country researched, because even the shared baseline (the swissuniversities list) is explicitly non-binding, and the two federal institutions add their own exam layer that the ten cantonal universities do not.
gaps: Whether individual Bachelor's programmes require a specific Matura Schwerpunktfach from Swiss-track applicants was not independently confirmed this pass.
The precise legal instrument (cantonal statute vs. university regulation) behind St. Gallen's 25% foreign-student quota was not identified beyond HSG's own 'limited by law' framing.
Exactly which applicant subgroup EPFL's GPA-ranking mechanism touches when its 3,000-place cap is oversubscribed was not fully disambiguated in the source reviewed.

Full current-cycle Turkey-specific admission criteria at Lausanne, Neuchatel, Lucerne and Fribourg individually were not independently swept this pass -- this research sampled ETHZ, EPFL, UZH, Bern, Geneva and St. Gallen directly, plus the swissuniversities aggregate covering all 12 institutions.

system_university_programme_override_mod.explanation: Layer 0 (joint federal-cantonal): recognition of the gymnasiale Maturitat itself, via EDK/CDIP's MAR regulation paired with the Federal Council's MAV ordinance -- binding nationally; no university can redefine what counts as a valid Matura. Layer 1 (inter-cantonal coordination, non-binding): CDIP's exam-free-access commitment for Matura holders, and swissuniversities' shared country-by-country foreign-qualification reference -- both are coordination/standard-setting layers every institution consults but that explicitly do not themselves decide any individual case ('the relevant legal provisions of each university are decisive'). Layer 2 (institution type): universities/ETHs (Matura-track) versus Fachhochschulen (Berufsmatura-track) run genuinely different admission logics, not merely different thresholds. Layer 3 (individual institution): this is where Switzerland diverges most sharply from every other country in this package -- ETH Zurich and EPFL each layer their own entrance-exam requirement on top of the shared swissuniversities baseline (confirmed concretely: the same Turkish diploma package sufficient on its own at 10 cantonal universities still requires ETHZ's Reduced Entrance Examination), while St. Gallen layers a quota-driven selection procedure that applies regardless of qualification strength. Layer 4 (linguistic region): for Medicine and related restricted fields, German/Italian-speaking institutions use EMS while French-speaking institutions use a structurally different post-entry exam -- a grouping axis that cuts across, rather than nesting inside, the institution-by-institution layer. Layer 5 (programme): subject-prerequisite content embedded in the foreign-qualification recognition template itself, plus narrower programme-specific rules (Basel's Sport, Exercise and Health provisions). ORYN should never present a Layer 3, 4, or 5 fact as if it were a Layer 0 or Layer 1 national fact.

matrix_row.main_application_architecture: Fully decentralized -- no shared application or registration platform of any kind; each of the ~12 universities/ETHs (plus a separate Fachhochschule/HES sector) runs its own direct online application process and decision
matrix_row.central_platform: None for applications. swissuniversities (the universities' own umbrella association) publishes a shared, annually-revised country-by-country admission-requirements reference that member institutions draw on, but it is not a portal and makes no admission decisions ('the relevant legal provisions of each university are decisive')
matrix_row.direct_applications_possible: Yes -- it is the only route; there is no centralized alternative. Every applicant applies directly and separately to each institution
matrix_row.application_choice_limits: No shared numeric cap (no UCAS-5/NL-2/Germany-12 equivalent) -- apply to as many of the 12 institutions as practical/financial capacity allows, each a separate fee+process. Partial exception: one EMS sitting is usable across the whole EMS university consortium. EPFL's new 2025-29 cap of 3,000 first-year places can convert EPFL specifically into a ranked/competitive process for non-Swiss-qualification applicants if oversubscribed
matrix_row.predicted_grades_role: No native Swiss-Matura predicted-grade artifact; cantonal Matura finals commonly sit May-June, after the commonly-cited ~30 April deadline, suggesting even Swiss-track applicants may apply pre-results (unconfirmed system-wide). Foreign IB/A-Level/AP applicants do submit predicted/interim grades operationally (e.g. St. Gallen accepts a 'half-year report' pending the final certificate)
matrix_row.subject_prerequisites: For foreign qualifications: a recurring shared template (documented directly in ETH's own country-by-country requirements) -- last 2-3 years must show mathematics, a science, and the language of instruction as examined subjects (commonly ~70% average) plus four more subjects from a defined list. For Swiss-Matura holders, programme-level Schwerpunktfach requirements were not independently confirmed this pass
matrix_row.standardized_tests: No SAT/ACT-equivalent. EMS (Eignungstest Medizin) is the dominant instrument -- Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary Medicine/Chiropractic at Basel/Bern/Fribourg/Zurich/USI/ETH Zurich, triggered when demand exceeds places by more than 20%. Geneva/Lausanne/Neuchatel use a different, post-entry first-year selection instead of EMS for the same fields. ETHZ and EPFL each also run their own bespoke Reduced/Comprehensive entrance exam for non-automatically-recognized foreign diplomas
matrix_row.language_proof: Overwhelmingly German/French/Italian (the instruction language), not English -- genuinely distinct from Bachelor's-level Netherlands/Germany. Commonly C1 CEFR in the instruction language; Geneva requires French B2+. Confirmed exception: St. Gallen's Economic Sciences Assessment Year can be completed entirely in English
matrix_row.essays_motivation: Not required for the general route anywhere reviewed. St. Gallen's foreign-applicant-only selection procedure includes a ~10-minute recorded video interview on motivation/interests, not a written essay
matrix_row.recommendations: Not a standard Bachelor's admission requirement in any official source reviewed
matrix_row.extracurricular_role: Not a documented factor in any official source reviewed for the general admission route
matrix_row.conditional_offers: Narrower/more procedural sense than NL/UK -- no distinctly-named conditional-offer status found generally; final certificate is submitted once available, no later than course start. Medicine/Dentistry/Veterinary Medicine/Chiropractic show a clearer eligible-vs-admitted split via EMS or the French-region first-year exam
matrix_row.restricted_programmes: At least four structurally distinct mechanisms, not one: EMS pre-entry test (most regions), French-region post-entry first-year exam (same fields), EPFL's new 2025-29 blanket 3,000-place Bachelor's-wide cap, and St. Gallen's 25%-by-law foreign-student quota with its own selection procedure (nationality/certificate-origin-gated, all fields)
matrix_row.turkiye_meb_direct_entry_complexity: High and university-specific. Only Anadolu Lisesi Diplomasi/Fen Lisesi Diplomasi are named as recognized; at 10 of 12 institutions the diploma plus proof of admission to a Turkish university programme is sufficient with no extra exam, but ETHZ requires its own Reduced Entrance Examination even then (Comprehensive if that proof is missing) -- no exam-free pathway exists at ETHZ for this qualification type. EPFL treats Turkey as a non-EU/EFTA/UK country requiring its own entrance exam. IB/A-Level/AP held alongside the Turkish diploma is evaluated under the easier, potentially exam-free IB/A-Level criteria instead
matrix_row.dominant_counselor_risk: Assuming a diploma's presence on swissuniversities' country list, or a Turkish applicant's plain MEB-system Lise diploma, establishes admission -- it establishes eligibility at most, is frequently insufficient on its own (a Turkish-university-admission certificate is usually also required), and at ETHZ/EPFL specifically a university-set entrance exam still applies on top even when every documentary condition is met. A second, equally live risk: assuming 'numerus clausus' means one mechanism nationally, when Switzerland runs at least four genuinely different ones (EMS, French-region first-year exams, EPFL's new capacity cap, St. Gallen's foreign quota) side by side

unresolved_questions: Whether individual Bachelor's programmes require a specific Matura Schwerpunktfach (subject specialization) from Swiss-track applicants, analogous to the Netherlands' profiel mapping -- not independently confirmed this pass.

Whether 'one year of completed accredited home-country university study' is a verbatim-confirmed ETH Zurich transfer pathway or only a secondary/consultancy characterization -- only secondary sourcing was found.

The precise legal instrument (cantonal statute vs. university regulation) behind St. Gallen's 25% foreign-student quota -- confirmed as 'limited by law' on HSG's own page, but the specific statute was not identified.

Exactly which applicant subgroup EPFL's new GPA-ranking mechanism touches when its 3,000-place cap is oversubscribed -- EPFL's own communications were not fully disambiguated on this point in the source reviewed.

Whether YKS scores play any explicit, named role anywhere in Swiss recognition of Turkish qualifications, beyond their indirect role in producing the Turkish-university-admission certificate -- no Swiss source named YKS directly.
Whether portfolio-based Bachelor's admission exists at Swiss university level (as opposed to Fachhochschule level) for art/design/music programmes -- out of scope this pass.
The precise EMS registration deadline and how it relates to each EMS-consortium university's own general application deadline -- not independently confirmed to the day.

Full current-cycle admission criteria for Turkish applicants at Lausanne, Neuchatel, Lucerne, and Fribourg specifically -- this pass sampled ETHZ, EPFL, UZH, Bern, Geneva, and St. Gallen directly, plus the swissuniversities aggregate covering all 12; a dedicated per-university sweep of the remaining institutions' own Turkey-specific pages was out of scope.

A_admissions_architecture.primary_application_route: The Central Applications Office (CAO) is the near-universal centralized platform for EU/EFTA/UK-fee-status applicants applying to full-time undergraduate courses at Irish Higher Education Institutions (universities, Technological Universities, and other HEIs). CAO is a private company (Central Applications Office Ltd., registered in Ireland, based in Galway) jointly owned and operated by the participating HEIs, not a government body. Critically, CAO is NOT merely a registration/routing layer like Studielink or UCAS: for the large majority of 'points' (non-restricted) courses, CAO's own system computes a ranked list of all eligible applicants by their Leaving Certificate (or equivalent) points score and automatically issues offers to the highest-ranked applicants up to the number of places the HEI has specified for that course code, with no separate per-application human review at the university for most courses. Admission decisions remain formally and legally the HEIs' — each HEI sets the entry requirements, subject prerequisites, and place count per course code and instructs CAO how to process it (Citizens Information, a statutory information body: 'The HEIs decide who gets places on their courses and they tell the CAO to make offers to successful candidates... all decisions on admissions are made by the individual institutions and not by the CAO') — but the moment-to-moment ranking/allocation execution is a shared, centrally-run computation, not an act of individual human review per application for standard courses.
A_admissions_architecture.centralized_or_decentralized: Hybrid, but a structurally different hybrid from the UK, Netherlands, or Italy. Application processing AND the points-ranking/allocation execution are centralized in CAO's shared system for the large majority of courses; setting entry requirements, subject prerequisites, and per-course place counts remains decentralized to each HEI, which then instructs CAO how to process its own course codes. Restricted-application courses (Medicine, Art & Design, Architecture, etc.) layer an HEI-run early assessment (portfolio, interview, aptitude test) on top of this shared points mechanism rather than replacing it. Non-EU/international applicants generally sit outside this architecture entirely, applying direct to each HEI's own international admissions office.
major_application_platforms: CAO (Central Applications Office) — the required route for essentially all EU/EFTA/UK-fee-status full-time undergraduate applicants; some non-EU applicants may also be instructed by a specific HEI to apply through CAO (e.g., for visa-timing reasons), but this is HEI-specific, not the default for non-EU applicants

Each HEI's own direct international-admissions portal (e.g., UCD's www.ucd.ie/apply, Trinity's course-specific 'Non-EU Application' pages) — the default route for non-EU/international-fee-status applicants
A_admissions_architecture.direct_university_application_possible: Yes, and it is the DEFAULT (not the exception) for non-EU/international-fee-status applicants: UCD's own registry states non-EU applicants 'apply direct to UCD, rather than through the Central Applications Office (CAO) like EU applicants,' and Trinity's non-EU applicants apply via a course-specific 'Non-EU Application' link with a separate per-course application fee. For EU/EFTA/UK-fee-status applicants, direct application in place of CAO is generally NOT available for CAO-listed courses — UCD states explicitly that EU-fee-status applicants 'will only be admitted through the Central Applications Office (CAO) system,' in line with CAO and National University of Ireland (NUI) matriculation regulations. Fee status, not nationality alone, is the operative test (e.g., UK-citizen applicants who meet an Irish/EU residency requirement are still assessed for EU fees and must apply via CAO).
A_admissions_architecture.application_limit_if_any: Via CAO: up to 10 Level 8 (Honours Bachelor) course preferences and up to 10 Level 7/6 (Ordinary Bachelor / Higher Certificate) preferences — two separate ranked lists — per Citizens Information's official walkthrough of the CAO application form ('You can choose Level 8, Level 7, and Level 6 courses. You can add up to 10 courses at any (or all) of these levels'). No numerus-fixus-style cap on how many 'selective' or restricted courses may be chosen was found — unlike the Netherlands' 2-numerus-fixus cap, Ireland does not appear to need an equivalent rule, because virtually all Level 8 courses (not just a capped subset) already run through the same unified points-ranking mechanism. Direct non-EU applications to a given HEI are typically made and paid for per-course (e.g., Trinity: a separate EUR 55 fee per course application).
A_admissions_architecture.parallel_application_rules: A single CAO account holds one ranked list per level (Level 8; Level 7/6), covering all HEI/course combinations the applicant is interested in; CAO processes each course code according to that HEI's own instructed criteria, and the applicant receives a single unified stream of offers (by round) reflecting the highest-ranked eligible preference at each stage — structurally different from the non-EU/direct route, where an applicant submits and pays for a fully separate application per HEI (and sometimes per course) with no shared ranked-preference mechanism at all.
A_admissions_architecture.scope: platform (CAO mechanics) / national (EU-fee-status applicants' effective requirement to use CAO derives from joint HEI/NUI matriculation regulation, not a single statute naming CAO itself)

B_qualification_eligibility.recognition_mechanism: Two layers, structurally parallel to the Netherlands' Nuffic/university split. (1) QQI (Quality and Qualifications Ireland) hosts NARIC Ireland (the National Academic Recognition Information Centre, part of the ENIC-NARIC network) and publishes comparability statements comparing a foreign qualification to an Irish National Framework of Qualifications (NFQ) award-type and level. QQI is explicit that this is advisory only: 'a comparability statement only provides advice and is not a legal document... decisions on recognising your qualification for employment, training or educational purposes will be made by the individual employer, competent authority or education and training admissions staff.' (2) For the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK route specifically, the participating HEIs jointly author and agree a separate, more operational document — 'Agreed Entry Requirements for EU/EFTA/UK Applicants' — which sets country-by-country matriculation requirements and Indicative Points Score (IPS) conversion tables; the document itself states 'This document is produced jointly by the participating institutions and not CAO,' reinforcing that CAO executes but does not author admissions policy. For non-EU/EFTA/UK applicants (including Turkish nationals), neither of these documents applies directly — each HEI sets and publishes its own recognition/entry criteria independently (see Türkiye section).
B_qualification_eligibility.baseline_qualification_expectation: For the Leaving Certificate itself (and, via the joint EU/EFTA/UK document, for other European qualifications), the operative baseline is 'matriculation' — a floor separate from and prior to competitive points ranking. The CAO EU/EFTA/UK Guidelines state the general Level 8 matriculation requirement is either (a) 6 subjects at Ordinary-level grade O6 or better, including 2 at Higher-level grade H5 or better, or (b) the same 6-subject O6 floor including 3 at H5 or better. Level 7/6 matriculation is normally 5 subjects at O5 or better. English must normally be included among the recognised subjects in all cases. The document is explicit that meeting this floor does NOT secure a place: 'entry to undergraduate courses in Ireland, and especially Level 8, is competitive and attainment of the minimum eligibility criteria does not guarantee a place. A points scoring system is in operation.'
B_qualification_eligibility.subject_prerequisites_general: Programme-specific, not decorative, but layered onto an à-la-carte Leaving Certificate rather than a Dutch-style fixed subject-combination ('profiel') structure — Irish students choose roughly 7-8 subjects individually from a wide list, without being forced into one of a small number of named national tracks. Many programmes (particularly STEM, Business, Economics, and health-science fields) require or strongly reward Higher Level Mathematics; a small number (e.g., Medicine, Veterinary Medicine, Engineering) specify additional science/maths subjects. See dedicated subject_prerequisites section.
B_qualification_eligibility.equivalency_process: For the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK route: the jointly-agreed Guidelines document supplies country-specific matriculation tables and IPS conversion for roughly 30 European countries plus the International Baccalaureate, European Baccalaureate, and Ukrainian qualifications; qualifications outside this list (Appendix II: 'Non-EU qualifications,' e.g., African and Australian examination systems) are given only as indicative, non-binding guidance, with final assessment reserved to 'the relevant Higher Education Institution following receipt and verification of the applicant's official documentation.' For the non-EU/direct route: each HEI runs its own equivalency process; UCD and UCC both publish detailed per-programme, per-country tables (see Türkiye section) while Trinity instead names a short list of internationally portable qualifications (A-Level, IB, US High School Diploma + SAT/ACT) accepted for direct entry, routing everything else to its Foundation Programme.
B_qualification_eligibility.university_discretion: Substantial, and structurally central to this system in a way distinct from the Netherlands. Within the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK route, HEIs retain the power to set subject requirements and, crucially, the annual place count per course code that determines that year's emergent points cutoff — the same Leaving Certificate points total can be sufficient for one HEI's course and insufficient for another's, purely as a function of that course's specific applicant demand and place count. Within the non-EU/direct route, discretion is even more visible and openly documented: UCD, UCC, and Trinity apply materially different policies to the identical input qualification (a Turkish Lise Diplomasi) — see Türkiye section for the specific, sourced contrast.

credentials_covered.turkiye_meb: Turkish 'Lise Diploması' / 'Devlet Lise Diploması' (state general secondary school diploma) is NOT processed through the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK points system at all, since Turkey falls outside that document's scope; each HEI sets its own direct-entry policy — see dedicated Türkiye section below, which documents a genuine, sourced split between HEIs that accept it directly at a sufficient percentage (UCD, UCC) and one that does not accept it for direct entry at all (Trinity).
credentials_covered.ib_diploma: Processed through the CAO points system when an EU/EFTA/UK-fee-status applicant presents it: the Guidelines document gives an explicit IB-score-to-Indicative-Points-Score conversion table (e.g., 45 points = 600 IPS; 24 points = 350 IPS), plus a 25-point Higher Level Mathematics bonus (grade 4+) mirroring the Leaving Certificate bonus. Critically, CAO uses ACTUAL final IB results only, obtained directly from the IB organisation once the applicant's IB coordinator grants CAO access — not predicted grades (see Predicted grades section). For non-EU/direct applicants, IB is one of the qualifications Trinity names as accepted for direct undergraduate entry without a Foundation Programme.
credentials_covered.a_levels: Same treatment pattern as IB within the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK route (own country/qualification-specific matriculation and IPS table; GCSE English grade 4/C or better generally satisfies the English-language requirement). For non-EU/direct applicants, A-Levels are named by Trinity (and implicitly by UCD, which routes A-Level/IB applicants to separate curriculum-specific pages rather than the Lise-percentage table) as an accepted direct-entry qualification.
credentials_covered.ap_plus_us_diploma: Not addressed in the CAO EU/EFTA/UK Guidelines' main country tables (the US is outside EU/EFTA/UK scope), but explicitly named by Trinity as an accepted direct non-EU entry route ('US High School Diploma with SAT or ACT'), and appears as an alternative route within UCD's Turkey-specific table for Turkish applicants who supplement a lower Lise Diplomasi percentage with a qualifying SAT score.
credentials_covered.french_bac: Covered within the CAO EU/EFTA/UK Guidelines' country-by-country tables (France has its own dedicated section with matriculation and IPS conversion) for EU-fee-status applicants; not independently verified for the non-EU/direct route in this research pass.
credentials_covered.german_abitur: Covered within the CAO EU/EFTA/UK Guidelines' country-by-country tables (Germany has its own dedicated section) for EU-fee-status applicants; not independently verified for the non-EU/direct route in this research pass.

turkiye_applicant_view.standard_diploma_sufficient_for_direct_e: Genuinely, sharply university-specific — the most non-uniform pattern found across the countries researched so far. Turkish nationals fall entirely outside the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK points system (Turkey is absent from that jointly-agreed document's ~30-country scope), so each HEI independently decides whether a plain Lise Diplomasi suffices. UCD (official Turkey-specific admissions table, 2026 entry) publishes direct per-programme percentage thresholds ranging from 67% Lise (e.g., BA Arts, History, English Literature) up to 100% Lise (e.g., Commerce, BSc Business, Computer Science, Engineering Omnibus, Architecture) — OR alternative routes combining a lower Lise percentage with either a partial Turkish university degree GPA (e.g., '71% Lise & 3.0/4.0 in degree') or a qualifying SAT score (e.g., '83% Lise & 1220 SAT'). UCC similarly publishes a tiered direct-entry system (67% / 85% / 90% Lise depending on programme competitiveness band) but additionally requires a passing result in Turkey's national university entrance exam (UCC's own page names it 'Lisans Yerleştirme Sınavı (LYS)' — the pre-2018 exam name, now superseded by YKS; this may indicate the page has not been updated to current Turkish exam terminology, a genuine data-quality caution rather than a confirmed current requirement). Trinity College Dublin, by contrast, does NOT accept the plain Lise Diplomasi for direct undergraduate entry at all: its official Turkey page states accepted qualifications for direct application are 'GCE A Levels, International Baccalaureate, US High School Diploma with SAT or ACT' only, and directs applicants without one of these to its International Foundation Programme. A Turkish applicant's eligibility for direct entry therefore cannot be assumed from one Irish university to the next.
turkiye_applicant_view.additional_qualifications_commonly_requi: Two patterns confirmed: (1) at HEIs like Trinity that do not accept the plain Lise Diplomasi at all, a full IB Diploma, A-Levels, or a US High School Diploma with a qualifying SAT/ACT score is required for direct entry; (2) at HEIs like UCD that do accept the plain Lise Diplomasi, applicants below the top percentage band can alternatively qualify via a qualifying SAT score layered on top of a lower Lise percentage, or via partial completion (GPA-based) of a Turkish university degree. UCC additionally documents accepted alternates including an 'Ön-Lisans Diplomasi' (associate degree) for its highest-competitiveness programme band.
turkiye_applicant_view.ap_ib_a_level_impact: Materially simplifies the picture, consistent with the pattern in every other country in this research package. At Trinity, IB/A-Level/AP-supported qualifications are the PRIMARY accepted direct-entry route for Turkish applicants (the plain Lise Diplomasi is not independently sufficient there at all). At UCD, IB and A-Level applicants are directed to separate, curriculum-specific entry-requirement pages rather than the Lise-percentage table, implying more standardised treatment than the country-specific negotiation a plain-diploma applicant faces.
turkiye_applicant_view.national_entrance_exam_relevance: Genuinely unresolved and inconsistent across the three universities sourced. UCC's published table names Turkey's national university entrance exam (under the outdated 'LYS' label) as a requirement layered on top of the Lise Diplomasi percentage for direct entry. UCD's detailed, programme-by-programme Turkey table makes no mention of YKS/LYS at all — its direct-entry routes are Lise-percentage-only, Lise+degree-GPA, or Lise+SAT. This should be recorded as a genuine, live cross-university difference — not resolved into one system-wide answer — and treated with additional caution given UCC's apparent use of superseded exam terminology (LYS was replaced by YKS in the 2018 Turkish exam reform).
turkiye_applicant_view.foundation_year_common: Yes, and it is the explicit, named fallback route at multiple HEIs for Turkish (and other non-EU) applicants who do not meet a given university's direct-entry bar. Trinity's International Foundation Programme is the stated route for any Turkish applicant without A-Level/IB/US-diploma-with-SAT/ACT. UCD separately operates an International Foundation Year 'for many programmes' for applicants who do not meet direct-entry requirements. Beyond the flagship universities, TU Dublin, Dublin City University, University College Cork, University of Limerick, Technological University of the Shannon, and private-partner colleges (e.g., Dublin International Foundation College, OnCampus Ireland) all publish International Foundation Programmes aimed at this population, typically one year long, with IELTS entry thresholds commonly cited around 4.5-5.5, some with guaranteed progression to a named degree programme on successful completion (e.g., TU Dublin).
turkiye_applicant_view.recognition_centralized_or_university_sp: University-specific, more decisively than in any other country covered by this research package so far. There is no CAO-run or QQI-run centralized Turkey-specific points conversion at all for non-EU-status Turkish applicants (QQI/NARIC Ireland's comparability statements are general and advisory, not admissions decisions, and CAO's jointly-agreed Guidelines document explicitly excludes non-EU/EFTA/UK qualifications from its scope). Each HEI independently authors, publishes, and can revise its own Turkey-specific (or Turkey-silent, in Trinity's case) policy. A Turkish applicant's acceptance at one Irish university carries no implication for any other.

academic_evidence_used.transcript_role: Within the CAO/points route, no separate transcript submission or holistic review occurs for standard courses — the points score is computed directly and mechanically from the applicant's official Leaving Certificate (or equivalent) results record, which CAO itself retrieves/receives from the State Examinations Commission (or, for IB, directly from the IB organisation once access is granted). Within the non-EU/direct route, a full transcript is a required, individually-reviewed document (alongside references, SOP, and English proficiency evidence).
academic_evidence_used.native_grades_handling: Within the CAO/EU-EFTA-UK route, each qualification type is read on its own scale via a jointly-agreed, qualification-specific conversion to a common 'Indicative Points Score' (IPS) — the Leaving Certificate's own H1-H8/O1-O8 scale IS the points scale (no conversion needed), while IB, A-Level, and ~30 other European qualifications each have their own explicit IPS conversion table in the Guidelines document; qualifications are never blended (the document states 'Two different examination types cannot be combined for scoring purposes'). Within the non-EU/direct route, native grades (e.g., a Turkish Lise Diploması percentage) are read directly against university-published percentage thresholds rather than converted to a universal GPA.
academic_evidence_used.predicted_grades_role: None, within the CAO/points route — see dedicated predicted_grades section; this holds even for IB/A-Level applicants whose home curricula natively produce predicted grades. Predicted grades DO appear to play a role within the separate non-EU/direct-to-university route (see predicted_grades section).
academic_evidence_used.final_grades_role: Central and load-bearing for the CAO/points route: no offer for a standard course issues before actual final results are known, and the entire Round system is sequenced around the Leaving Certificate results-release date (21 August for the 2026 cycle). For the non-EU/direct route, final results are ultimately required to confirm/finalise a place, but an offer built on predicted or in-progress results can be made earlier (see predicted_grades and conditional_vs_unconditional sections).
academic_evidence_used.external_exams_role: The Leaving Certificate, for CAO points purposes, is entirely externally/nationally set and marked by the State Examinations Commission — unlike the Dutch VWO diploma's mixed school-set (schoolexamen) plus national (centraal examen) composite, there is no school-set continuous-assessment component feeding into the CAO points score for the mainstream Leaving Certificate. (The separate Leaving Certificate Applied (LCA) track is a distinct, non-points-scored qualification and should not be conflated with the mainstream, CAO-points-scored Leaving Certificate.)
academic_evidence_used.course_rigor_signal: Read through explicit subject-level/grade-level prerequisites published per course (commonly a named minimum Higher Level Mathematics grade, sometimes a lab science) rather than a general 'rigor' holistic judgment; see subject_prerequisites section.
academic_evidence_used.standardized_tests: HPAT-Ireland (Medicine, all 6 medical schools) is the one nationally mandatory aptitude test within the domestic system; no SAT/ACT role within the CAO/points route. See dedicated standardized_tests section.

predicted_grades.are_used: Not within the CAO/points route, for any applicant category, in any curriculum. Ireland's system is explicitly described in official and semi-official sources as 'post-qualification admissions' — offers for standard courses are computed and issued only after actual final results are known. This is confirmed at its strongest for IB applicants specifically: the CAO Guidelines instruct May-sitting IB candidates to grant CAO direct electronic access to their ACTUAL final IB results once released, and CAO uses only that real result for points calculation — the IB's own native predicted-grade artifact (used operationally by UK/UCAS and, per this research package's Netherlands findings, by Dutch universities) plays no role in the CAO points process at all.
predicted_grades.where: Predicted grades DO appear to be used within the separate, HEI-run non-EU/direct-to-university application route: Trinity's general international undergraduate admissions page lists acceptable supporting documentation as 'Final high school exam results, OR Predicted Scores provided by your school' — explicitly naming predicted scores as sufficient at the application stage for non-EU applicants (who commonly present IB or A-Level qualifications, both of which natively produce predicted grades).
predicted_grades.by_whom: Where used (non-EU/direct route only): issued by the applicant's own school/teachers under the rules of their home qualification (IB, A-Level), not generated or estimated by any Irish body. Within the CAO/points route, there is no predicted-grade artifact of any kind, native or foreign, that CAO itself acts upon.
predicted_grades.for_what: Where used, to allow a non-EU applicant's file to be assessed and an offer considered ahead of final results being known — functionally the same purpose predicted grades serve in the UK, but confined (on the evidence found this pass) to the non-EU/direct pipeline rather than being a system-wide Irish mechanism.
predicted_grades.conditional_offer_relationship: Not established within the CAO/points route in the predicted-grade sense (there is no forward-looking target grade to be conditional upon; see conditional_vs_unconditional_admission section for the different, narrower senses of 'conditional' that do exist there). Plausibly linked within the non-EU/direct route — a Trinity-style application built on predicted scores would logically require some later confirmation step once final results are issued — but this research pass did not locate an explicit Irish HEI offer-letter example using UCAS-style 'conditional offer' terminology; this should be treated as a reasonable inference from the accepted-documentation list, not a directly sourced confirmation.
predicted_grades.final_result_requirement: Yes, universally — even within the non-EU/direct route where predicted scores are accepted at application stage, actual final results are ultimately required before enrolment. Within the CAO/points route, final results are required before any offer is even issued, not merely before enrolment is finalised.

conditional_vs_unconditional_admission.concept_exists: Yes, but in a materially narrower and differently-structured sense within the CAO/points route than in the UK or Netherlands, plus a separate, more UK-like sense that appears to exist only within the non-EU/direct route.
conditional_vs_unconditional_admission.explanation: Within the CAO/points route: there is no predicted-grade-conditional offer at all (no offer issues until actual results are known — see predicted_grades). What resembles 'conditionality' here is purely sequencing/logistics, not a forward-looking academic target: restricted-course early assessment (portfolio, interview, HPAT) can occur months before Leaving Certificate results, but the resulting points-based offer still only issues once actual results are known and combined with that earlier assessment score — the early step does not itself constitute an offer. Round A/Round Zero (mature, deferred, graduate-entry medicine, QQI/FET, some non-EU/visa-timing applicants) can receive offers before the main Leaving Certificate results date specifically because these applicant categories typically already hold final, already-known results from an earlier period — not because a prediction is being acted upon. Within the non-EU/direct route: Trinity's acceptance of 'Predicted Scores' as application-stage evidence implies a genuine, UK-like conditional-offer mechanism (offer contingent on achieving a stated final result) is operating, though this research pass did not verify an actual offer-letter example using that terminology.

subject_prerequisites.pattern: Real and programme-specific, but structurally different from the Netherlands' VWO 'profielen' model: the Leaving Certificate has no fixed, small set of named national subject-combination tracks — students choose roughly 7-8 subjects individually (subject to school-timetabling practicalities), and programmes then publish their own specific subject/grade prerequisites on top of that open structure, most commonly a named minimum Higher Level Mathematics grade, and for some fields a lab science. Higher Level Mathematics carries a national +25 CAO-points bonus (for grade H6 or above) that functions as a strong incentive layer distinct from, and additional to, any hard subject requirement a specific course sets.
subject_prerequisites.scope: programme (individual course codes set their own subject/grade prerequisites; the national Leaving Certificate structure itself imposes no fixed subject-combination requirement analogous to VWO profielen)
illustrative_examples: UCD's non-EU entry table shows explicit, programme-differentiated Mathematics minimums: 'C2 3rd level / 4.5 Lise' for Business/Computer Science/Engineering-track programmes, 'B3 3rd level' for the Engineering Omnibus, 'D1 3rd level / 2 Lise' for Economics/Social Science/Agricultural Science programmes — i.e., the required Mathematics standard is set per programme, not uniformly.

CAO's own EU/EFTA/UK Guidelines note generally that 'for some HEIs Mathematics is required for matriculation' in addition to the general floor, and that 'there are specific subject requirements for most courses' beyond matriculation.
Medicine and Veterinary Medicine require specific lab-science subjects (e.g., UCD's non-EU Veterinary Medicine entry specifies a Chemistry requirement) alongside the general Mathematics standard.
Higher Level Mathematics' +25-point CAO bonus is applied nationally regardless of programme, but only actually lifts an applicant's total if Higher Level Mathematics is among their best 6 subjects.
subject_prerequisites.vwo_profielen_detail: Not applicable — Ireland has no equivalent fixed-track subject-combination structure. This is a genuine structural difference from the Netherlands worth naming explicitly: the Leaving Certificate is closer to an à-la-carte subject list (with matriculation-level and course-level constraints layered on afterward) than to a small number of named national profiles.

standardized_tests.mandatory_optional_status: No SAT/ACT-style general admissions test exists within the domestic CAO/points route.
